 1 Task Description
 One of the ways to model the static soil-structure interaction is to model the soil according to the Winkler assumption. This method is relatively simple to use but cannot take into consideration the shear deformations within the soil.
 One of the most accurate methods is to model the soil using 3D finite elements. This however requires a huge number of soil elements which in many cases can sever times exceed the number of elements needed for modeling of the structure itself, which is usually the main part of interest for structural engineers.
 In HASE module a sub-structuring technique, in which the structure will be represented using standard finite elements, while the soil will be modeled semi-analytically using the half-space theory, is adopted. The connection between the two substructures will be assured by stiff- ness/flexibility coefficients at the soil-structure interface nodes. This method overcomes the problems of the other two techniques. It takes into consideration the shear deformations within the soil and it does not require explicit discreet modeling of the entire soil domain.
 Based on the halfspace theory, module HASE calculates the stiffness matrix representing the soil part of the static soil-structure interaction system. The soil- structure interaction analysis itself is then preformed in module ASE, in which the soil stiffness matrix is linked with the structure part and the response of the entire system under the prescribed loads is calculated.
 Once the static analysis is finished, HASE can be used for post-processing to determine stresses and settlements of the half-space (soil) due to the supporting forces calculated in the static analysis. It is also possible to perform independent settlement analysis within HASE, where the loads are directly applied to the half- space.

Once the static analysis is finished, HASE can be used for post-processing to determine stresses and settlements of the half-space (soil) due to the supporting forces calculated in the static analysis. It is also possible to perform independent settlement analysis within HASE, where the loads are directly applied to the half- space..
 It is possible to define layered half-space with soil parameters and layer thickness varying in vertical as well as in the radial direction. Therefore each point at the soil-structure inter- face can have different soil-parameters associated to it. This is achieved by interpolating the soil-properties and layer thicknesses from the defined bore profiles. There are following inter- polation schemes available:
 1. CONS - Constant soil profile at all the points of the half-space
 2. QUAD - Bilinear interpolation of a separate system containing a discretised model of the soil
 3. COOR - Interpolation of bore profiles using weight functions
 4. LAYR - Interpolation of the soil properties from the 3D triangular prism mesh model of the layered half-space defined by the bore profile distribution on the half-space surface
 The stiffness matrix does not need to be full in order to be processed. Therefore, the influence of points which are far away from each other (i.e., their distance is above a predefined limit) can be ignored to reduce CPU time.
 In the basic version of HASE, the program processes halfspace problems for plane slab struc- tures. The halfspace for three-dimensional systems is only available in the expanded version.

The program HASE first determines the flexibility matrix. This describes the displacement of a point due to a force on the point k within the half-space. The inverse of the flexibility matrix is the stiffness matrix. The entire calculation consists of five main parts (Bellmann and Radmanovi´c [1]):
 1. Calculation of the soil-profile distribution in the plan view
 2. Calculation of the flexibility matrix
 Inversion and storage of the stiffness matrix
 4. Static calculation including structural elements
 5. Determination of the stresses in the soil due to the calculated displacements.
 The steps 1,2,3 and 5 are executed by HASE. The third step is the most costly in terms of CPU time, accounting for up to 90% of the entire CPU time. However, for a given system, Step 3 need only be calculated once.
 For a half-space analysis with a small or sparse stiffness matrix, Step 3 does not necessarily have to be performed by HASE.
 Requirements:

 Then ASE has to iteratively obtain stiffnesses from the half-space, but it can use the sparse solver much more efficiently and is therefore much faster for certain large systems. In this case, the inversion of the flexibility matrix in HASE can be switched off with CTRL SOLV NONL, because the flexibility matrix is not used. For an example, see hase2.dat.
 A previously generated half-space matrix can simply be reused after a modification to the system. A new calculation of the stiffness matrix is only necessary if the coordinates or the numbering of the contact nodes to the half-space have been changed.

The soil bore profiles position and inclinations are defined in AQUA with the record BORE. Stiffness and resistance soil properties as well as the layer disposition along the bore profile axis are defined using BLAY record. The start depth of the first layer of the bore profile should be on the surface of the half-space (record HALF item Z). If the half-space surface is below the start depth of a bore profile a warning message will appear. If the half-space surface is above the start depth of a bore profile an error message will appear.

 In the 2nd case (QUAD) an arbitrary mesh of QUAD elements (system 2) has to be defined. The contours of the soil profile are described by information stored at the nodes of this second mesh. The soil characteristics are then interpolated bilinearly from the QUAD elements of system 2 to the nodes of the structure in the primary system (structure node A is situated in QUAD element X of system 2; the soil characteristics of A are determined from the four corner profiles of the element X). In this way, irregular soil profile distributions can be defined easily. Also, the soil profile definition is independent of the numbering and organization of the structure contained in the primary system.
 In the 3rd case (COOR), vertical soil profiles are defined at coordinates (X1,Y1) to (Xnp,Ynp). Next, the soil characteristics of the nodes are calculated as the superposition of all bore profile properties c multiplied by a weight factor EP specified in the record HALF.  Fourth method (LAYR) first constructs the triangular mesh on the surface of the half-space from the defined bore-profiles (Figure 2.1a). Next this mesh is extruded along the axes of bore profiles to construct the three-dimensional mesh of triangular prisms, defining discreet soil (half-space) domain (Figure 2.1b). In this way soil-properties at the corner nodes of the triangular prism are exactly those defined by the corresponding BORE+BLAY record in AQUA. Stiffness and resistance properties within a prism are interpolated using hierarchical shape functions (linear in the radial, quadratic in the vertical direction). Variation of the soil-properties along the BORE axis defined in the BLAY record is preserved. Geometry of the 3D prism mesh is saved in an additional *CDB. The prisms are only used for the interpolation of the defined soil properties; they are not used for the computation of the stiffness matrix of the soil. Stresses and deformations and therefore the stiffness matrix are determined using the half- space theory (see Sections 2.4 and 2.5). All nodes that belong to the structure-soil interface (foundation plate, piles) must be entirely encompassed within defined half-space domain.
 Restrictions:
 • Minimum 3 bore profiles, whose start points describe a convex polygon.
 • For inclined bore profiles: intersection of the sides of prisms should be avoided.
 When specifying different soil characteristics in the plan view, the number of layers must be the same in all bore profiles. The layer thicknesses can vary, however. The values ES, MUE, PMAX, PMAL, C and PHI as well as the layer thicknesses are then interpolated according to either method 2, 3 or 4.
 If there is a large difference between the stiffness of two adjacent soil layers, numerical prob- lems may result. Then half-space theory is no longer applicable, and an error message is printed.

 Once the Boussinesq method is activated, HASE sets the minimal Poisson’s ratio to 0.2. The input BLAY ES is still interpreted as stiffness modulus Es! Also using a material input MNO in BLAY MNO, the value E in MAT...E is interpreted as stiffness property Es, nevertheless if MAT...MUE is defined or not.

Since the Poisson’s ration of the soil is hard to define and not a constant value, in most of the practical applications the Poisson’s ratio is directly taken into consideration by using the stiffness modulus Es instead of the elasticity modulus E (Smoltczyk [2]). For ν = 0 both moduli are formally identical:
 (1 − ν)
 $$Es = E * (1 + n)(1 - 2n) . (2.8)$$
 The vertical strains εz can now be obtained by simply dividing vertical stresses σz with stiffness modulus Es, i.e.
 σz(z)
 $$ez(z) = Es(z) . (2.9)$$
 This method is activated when Poisson’s ratio MUE in BLAY record is not defined or is equal to zero.

In addition to the vertical stiffness normally used in the description of the half-space, a hori- zontal stiffness can also be calculated and stored. This stiffness can be used to describe the horizontal fixities of the structure and must be given if no other horizontal fixities are defined.
 The horizontal stiffness is determined simply as a proportion of the vertical stiffness. If not specified in the record HALF no horizontal stiffness is stored.
 Vertical walls are not taken into account in the horizontal stiffness as they are shadowed for the more important z action - see next chapter. So horizontally only the lower bottom slabs work on friction as well as enbedded beams (external piles).
 A calculation of three-dimensional systems is possible only in the expanded version of HASE.

With the default HALF ZVAR AUTO also systems with quad halfspace contact on variable z level can be analyzed, see example hase3_variable_surface_level.dat
 Actually the halfspace theory is no longer valid exactly in such a case, but nevertheless the analysis with HASE also gives big advantages compared to a simple quad bedding. Because
 also in case of variable z level, e.g. a load on a bottom slab at z level 4m causes a settlement in a neighboring bottom slab at z level 8m, and the other way round, = interaction in the HASE stiffness coefficient method. HASE tries to scale the stiffnesses to get good results also if the quad halfspace contact acts on variable z levels.
 In principle, in case a quad bottom slab lies under the halfspace surface, all under 60 degree higher nodes above will not get a halfspace contact. According the following figure, from the lower bottom slab a shadow is assumed under an angle of 60 degree to switch off nodes above:
 The soil in the angle of the cellar wall and the upper slab (green shaded) is inactive and just follows the deformation of the upper slab and the wall. To check this effect of the ZVAR method please plot the bedding stress as iso-area and you will immediately see this shadowing.
 If no shadowing occurs, all bottom slabs work as if they would stand on the top of the halfspace. This es e.g. the case if the right abutment of a bridge has another l level as the left one but both lie on the surrounding terrain surface. So the program looks around a bottom slab if there are other higher bottom slabs around:
 - if yes, the deep bottom slab is assumed to lie inside the halfspace
 - if no, the bottom slab is assumed to lie on top of the surface (uses a separate surface level)
 So with HALF-Z you mainly define, which elements will definitely not get a halfspace contact (all elements above HALF-Z).

 In the following example you set HALF-Z to the level of the left bottom slab (red line). As in the nearer surrounding of the right bottom slab no other higher halfspace contact is found, a local halfspace surface is assumed there (green). The same happens at the middle support with enbedded piles. So this represents the brown environmental surface.

There are two ways to model model load introduction by means of piles in HASE – as internal HASE-piles (PILE) or as extended piles (XPIL).
 Internal HASE-piles are not discretized in the finite element system. They are a property of the halfspace and defined with command PILE. Example - hase8_intern_piles.dat
 Extended piles are real beam elements in the system and thus need not to be defined with command PILE. Example - hase22_abutment_extended_piles.dat

Internal HASE Piles are no ream beam elememts and may be included as part of the calcula- tion of the stiffness matrix at the halfspace surface. In the linear calculation, it is assumed that MANT times the total pile load is transferred by pile skin friction (literal MANT in record PILE) and the rest as point pressure at the foot of the pile.
 The part of load supported by skin friction is evenly distributed, relative to the soil stiffnesses along the pile, over the length of the pile and integrated numerically.
 Loads introduced within the half-space are calculated according to equation 2.5.
 Piles within the half-space can only be calculated in the expanded version of HASE.

Piles are defined as beam-elements in the system that lie below the halfspace surface. In HASE, the stiffnesses of all beam nodes are obtained using the formula 2.5.
 In HASE, it is possible to directly include the effects of soil bedding on a pile- bedded structure, where piles are modeled as discrete beam elements and are part of the structure. The GRP record can be used to select beam groups where stiffness values should be calculated within the halfspace. In contrast to the PILE functionality, which condenses the total effect of the pile to a single stiffness at the point where the pile is attached to the structure, each node along an extended pile represents explicit degrees of freedom within the halfspace. This allows bedding effects to be represented continuously along the pile.
 The effective soil stiffness properties along X-pile are always determined from the half-space stiffness defined using bore profiles.
 If additional nonlinear resistance effects along X-pile are to be considered, this can be done by one of the following:
 1. Definition of the nonlinear resistance properties for each individual pile directly. If you do not need to give an individual nonlinear effect to every pile, the second method is recommended! If you need individual nonlinear effects this can be achieved by:
 • defining bedding profiles containing nonlinear specific information using BORE + BBAX or BBLA
 assigning these profiles directly to the corresponding X-pile beams at system input
 The following X-pile nonlinear effects can be taken into account when performing a non- linear analysis in combination with ASE:
 • maximum pile skin friction along the pile C0 (see AQUA record BBAX)
 • maximum axial pile foot force PMAX (see AQUA record BBAX)
 • maximum transverse compression PMA1 and PMA2 (see AQUA record BBLA)
 2. Interpolation of the nonlinear resistance properties from the corresponding soil parame- ters of the defined bore profile distribution. The length of the piles within halfspace, the pile diameter and pile circumference are automatically taken into consideration for the evaluation of the pile specific values. This method is achieved by:

• maximum transverse compression PMA1 and PMA2 (see AQUA record BBLA). 2. Interpolation of the nonlinear resistance properties from the corresponding soil parame- ters of the defined bore profile distribution. The length of the piles within halfspace, the pile diameter and pile circumference are automatically taken into consideration for the evaluation of the pile specific values. This method is achieved by:.
 •
 defining the soil nonlinear resistance properties using AQUA records BORE and BLAY
 •
 interpolating these properties using one of four interpolation schemes described in Section 2.3
 The X-pile nonlinear resistance properties that are interpolated in this way are maximum pressure at pile foot (PMAX), maximum lateral pressure (PMAL), cohesion (C) and soil- pile friction angle.
 Method 2 is a preferred method for the definition of X-pile resistance properties. Example: hase21_kpp_extended_piles.dat

Two specific curves are explicitly labeled with Roman numerals “II” near the upper-right portion of the plot. The curve marked “II” appears to rise substantially and cross near the top around 14–16 MB for the largest x values. The following limits should be observed:
 Number of bore profiles : 999 Number of system nodes : 999999 Number of halfspace nodes : 65000 Greatest node number : 999999
 Further limits are imposed by HASE and also by the computer hardware.
 The stiffness matrix must be determined by inverting the flexibility matrix. In this case, the system of equations must be solved n times (where n = number of nodes in halfspace). By comparison, in ASE the system of equations must be solved for a load case only 1 time, but for m unknowns (for the plate this is m = 3n, as each node has 3 unknowns).
 Because the inversion step costs a lot of CPU time, it is executed only in-core, that means exclusively in the main memory. Therefore the number of nodes which can be calculated depends on the size of main memory available. It also depends on the band width of the system of equations. This can be reduced by lowering the influence radius with the record CTRL INFL. Reducing bandwidth naturally reduces CPU time. The memory requirements can be estimated with the following diagram. The curves I to IV show different influence radii:
 Curve I : Influence radius = 999m
 Curve II : Influence radius = 30% of the system dimension Curve III : Influence radius = 10% of the system dimension Curve IV : Influence radius = 3% of the system dimension
 A square plate with 16m16m and 4040 elements (4141 = 1681 nodes) needs approxi- mately 6 − 7MB main memory for an influence radius of 4.80m(= 30% of 16m). With 4MB main memory, the problem can be processed with a maximum influence radius of approxi- mately 3.00m.

The stiffness of the halfspace is saved by HASE in the file PROJECT.$E2.
 At the start of the following statics program (ASE), this $E2-file is read in using the command STEX. The stiffness of the superstructure is then combined with the stiffness matrix of the halfspace to form a total stiffness matrix. The system of equations is solved and saved as PROJEKT.$D1.
 The default argument of the STEX command is PROJECT.$E2, so the input of STEX without any argument is generally sufficient. Because the contact nodes of the halfspace are assigned external node numbers, any other $E2-file may alternatively be specified.
 In the following statics calculation, load cases can quickly be computed without having to re- solve the system of equations. The STEX command need only be specified once for multiple load cases. No group selection is allowed. If material values or similar values used as inputs to HASE are modified, the system of equations must be set up and solved again in HASE.

Input is written in text using the free format of the CADINP input language (see the general manual ’SOFiSTiK Basics’).
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

This table is a **record/field structure overview** for an input module in SOFiSTiK. It specifies how to interpret the file: the input is organized in **ordered blocks**, each terminated by an **END** record. Within a block, a specific **system** or **load case** is analyzed. The overall program terminates when it encounters an **empty block** denoted by **END/END**. It also notes that **HEAD, END, and PAGE** follow the general description in the SOFiSTiK manual section *“Basics”*.

The table consists of two columns: **Record** and **Items**, where each row names a **record type** and lists the expected **fields/parameters** (and their abbreviations). The record labels are:

- **CTRL**: contains options and values  
  - **OPT** (option identifier)  
  - **VAL** (associated value)

- **GRP**: defines a group selection with multiple identifiers and flags  
  - **NO** (group number/id)  
  - **VAL** (group-related value)  
  - **FOOT**, **RC**, **CC** (additional modifiers/coefficients; exact meaning depends on context in the manual)

- **HALF**: describes a symmetry/half-model definition or partition parameters  
  - **TYPE** (half-type)  
  - **PROF** (profile/model relation)  
  - **EP** (endpoint/parameter)  
  - **Z** (z-direction coordinate or index)  
  - **FAXX**, **FAXY**, **FAKZ** (directional factors)

- **BORE**: parameters for bore/embedded opening or similar foundation feature  
  - **NO** (feature id)

- **PILE**: parameters describing pile geometry/placement  
  - **X**, **Y** (plan coordinates)  
  - **D0** (initial diameter/size)  
  - **D** (diameter/size)  
  - **Z** (depth/position)  
  - **MANT** (mantling / surface layer parameter)  
  - **ZMAN** (depth/location of mantle)  
  - **PMAM**, **PMAF** (side resistance / factors or material resistance terms)  
  - **MNO** (mapping material/number to property set)  
  - **TITL** (title/label)

- **PLAS**: additional sizing/limits  
  - **PMAX** (maximum parameter/value)

- **LOAD**: begins definition of a load entry (load-case related)  
  - **NO** (load id)  
  - **PZ** (load parameter/value; likely vertical magnitude or scaling)

- **LC**: defines load case selection  
  - **NO** (load case id)  
  - **NAME** (load case name)  
  - **TITLE**/**TITL** (descriptive text)  
  - **STVZ** (load case variation/setting)

- **SELE**: selection related to a z-position  
  - **NO** (selection id)  
  - **Z** (z coordinate criterion)

- **SELP**: selection parameters tied to a load case and branching  
  - **Z** (z coordinate)  
  - **LCST** (load case status/type)  
  - **BRIC** (brick/segment selection id)  
  - **DX**, **DY** (offsets/dimensions)  
  - **HMIN** (minimum height/size)

- **ECHO**: controls output echoing  
  - **OPT** (echo option)  
  - **VAL** (echo value/level)

The table also includes a contextual note for HASE: **“Previously defined material values may be modified in HASE.”** This implies that some of the listed parameters (especially those linked via identifiers such as **MNO**, **PMAM/PMAF**, or material-related codes) may reference earlier definitions and can be overridden later within the HASE workflow, consistent with the block-based structure described above.

Previously defined material values may be modified in HASE.
 The input is ordered in blocks which are terminated by an END record. A particular system or a load case can be analyzed within each block. The program ends if an empty block (END/END) is found.
 The following records are defined:
 The records HEAD, END and PAGE are described in the general manual SOFiSTiK: ”Basics”.

The table defines a configuration “OPT” control block with multiple selectable parameters, and a corresponding “VAL” block that provides the numeric value for the chosen option(s). It is structured into four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**.

## Item: OPT (Control option)
Under **OPT**, the **Description** column lists the names of available control options that affect how the calculation is performed, particularly in the context of non-linear soil–structure interaction computations and stiffness/flexibility handling. The **Unit** column is not specified for these option selectors (shown as “—”), and the **Default** column is “—”, indicating that defaults may differ per sub-option or are defined in the detailed text rather than directly in the table.

The listed **OPT** sub-options are:

1. **INFL** – *Influence radius for band width reduction*  
   Controls a cutoff distance: Nodes farther apart than **INFL** do not influence each other. This can greatly reduce CPU time for large systems.  
   Additional context given: **Default = 999 m**.

2. **TOLS** – *Minimum stiffness cutoff*  
   Stiffnesses below a threshold relative to the maximum stiffness are not stored and are replaced by zero.  
   Additional context: **Default = 1.E-6**.

3. **GAUS** – *Number of Gauss points per integration layer*  
   Governs integration accuracy. The program may subdivide thick soil layers into thinner layers for better strain integration; increasing integration layers typically yields only a few-percent improvement in most cases.  
   Additional context: **Default: GAUS = 1, maximum value: GAUS = 3**.

4. **SOLV** – *0/Linear/Nonlinear control* for solving strategy  
   Determines whether linear/nonlinear parameters are stored and whether flexibility matrices are inverted to stiffness matrices. Different values change solver behavior:  
   - **SOLV 0**: switch off calculation, only store non-linear parameters for ASE (see record PLAS).  
   - **SOLV -** (no input): compute flexibility matrix and invert to stiffness (may take longer).  
   - **SOLV NONL**: avoid inversion of the flexibility matrix; ASE then iterates (may be faster overall).  
   (Exact default not stated in the table.)

5. **FAKU** – *Ignore tension caused by pile forces*  
   Affects how pile loads are treated in halfspace modeling, specifically for **HASE-piles** and not extended piles.  
   Additional context: By allowing a portion of load to transmit directly downward when pile foot rests on rigid subsoil, it can remove the resulting upward tension component. A special minimum value can be set with **FAKU -**; when **CTRL FAKU 1** is set, all pile forces (including skin friction) transmit downward as compression.

6. **WARN** – *Switch off error messages*  
   Controls whether error messages are suppressed. (No default provided in the table.)

## Item: VAL (Value of the option)
The **VAL** row indicates the **value** to be assigned to the selected **OPT** parameter. It shows no specific **Unit** (—) and no **Default** (—) because the numeric meaning depends on which OPT option is being set (e.g., meters for INFL, dimensionless cutoff for TOLS, integer for GAUS, keywords for SOLV, etc., per the contextual text above).

sections: 3.3 CTRL – Control of the Analysis Method

content:
See also: HALF, PLAS
 CTRL
 INFL Nodes which lie more than INFL m from each other have no influence on each other. With this option, the CPU time can be reduced drastically for big systems. Default = 999 m
 TOLS Stiffnesses which are smaller than TOLS times the maximum stiffness are not saved, but rather replaced by zero. Default = 1.E-6
 GAUS Number of Gauss points per integration layer
 The program automatically divides thick soil layers into thinner layers to produce a more accurate integration of the strains due to the stresses. A finer subdivision of these integration layers leads to improvements in accuracy of only few percent in most cases. Default: GAUS = 1, maximum value: GAUS=3
 SOLV CTRL SOLV 0 : to switch off the calculation to only store non-linear parameters for ASE (see record PLAS).
 CTRL SOLV - : without input to SOLV, HASE calculates the flexibility matrix and inverts it to a stiffness matrix (may take some time).
 CTRL SOLV NONL : works without inversion of the flexibility matrix. But ASE then has to iterate, see ASE STEX OPT ITER. May be quicker in total.
 FAKU Piles in the halfspace: Works only on PILE (HASE-piles) and not on extended piles (real beam elements):
 If a pile foot stands on a rigid subsoil, it transmits its load directly downward and not partially as tension upward (as the equation [1] for a load which acts in the halfspace interior would suggest). Based on the soil profile (the actual available stiffnesses), HASE automatically determines how much of the pile load is diverted directly downward. Then this part produces no tension upward. It is output as “faku” in the table of pile parameters. For special cases, a minimum value can be defined with FAKU - when CTRL FAKU 1 is set, that means all pile forces (also the skin friction forces) are transmitted downward as compression.

The table defines configurable parameters for a command or module that appears to control how “groups” are activated and how contact-related stiffness/friction effects are modeled—especially at a pile foot interface. It has five columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**.

1. **NR — Group number**  
   - **Purpose:** Selects which group(s) the option applies to.  
   - **Unit/format:** Shown as **–/LIT** (an internal indicator that the value is either a wildcard/marker “all” style or a list identifier).  
   - **Default:** **!** (meaning the value is required/unspecified by default).  
   - **Special value:** **ALL** selects all groups.

2. **VAL — Option**  
   - **Purpose:** Controls whether result output is produced and/or suppressed.  
   - **Unit:** **LIT** (list/type).  
   - **Default:** **FULL**.  
   - **Allowed options:**  
     - **OFF:** do not use (the option is inactive).  
     - **YES:** use the option but **no output** of the results.  
     - **FULL:** use the option and **output** the results.

3. **FOOT — X-pile foot radius**  
   - **Purpose:** Defines the effective pile foot size to simulate additional stiffness at the pile foot.  
   - **Unit:** **m** (meters).  
   - **Default:** **-1.0**.  
   - **Interpretation rule:**  
     - **Positive value:** treated directly as a radius in meters.  
     - **Negative value:** interpreted as a **multiplier** of the pile radius.  
   - **Context alignment:** The surrounding text states the pile foot diameter is normally **1.4 times** the pile diameter (or **−1.4** when specified as a multiplier). This table row provides the radius-based equivalent mechanism: negative values act as multipliers of the pile radius.

4. **RC — Contact radius (for the stiffness)**  
   - **Purpose:** Overrides contact radius values computed automatically by HASE, enabling user control of stiffness-related contact geometry.  
   - **Unit:** **m**.  
   - **Default:** **-** (no explicit default; value is typically computed unless overwritten).

5. **CC — Contact circumference (for nonlinear mantle friction)**  
   - **Purpose:** Overrides contact circumference values computed by HASE, targeting friction behavior on the pile mantle in nonlinear conditions.  
   - **Unit:** **m**.  
   - **Default:** **-** (computed automatically unless RC/CC are explicitly provided).

Overall, the table supports: (a) selecting affected groups (NR/ALL behavior), (b) choosing whether results are output (VAL), and (c) optionally overriding pile-foot and contact geometry parameters (FOOT, RC, CC). The auxiliary context clarifies that specifying **RC** and **CC** allows bypassing HASE’s automatic contact geometry calculations, and that **FOOT** can be entered either directly (positive) or as a multiplier via a negative sign.

See also: CTRL
 GRP
 All elements are used if nothing is input. When there is input, only the specified groups get activated.
 To simulate the effects of additional stiffness at the pile foot, the (positive) diameter of the pile foot can be specified with FOOT. Alternatively, the pile foot diameter can be specified as a multiple of the pile diameter (where the pile diameter is calculated as an equivalent diameter, from the pile cross-section area), in which case the FOOT value is flagged with a minus sign. The default pile footing is 1.4 times the pile diameter, or −1.4.
 With the input of the options RC and CC the user is able to overwrite the values of the contact radius and contact circumference which are computed by HASE automatically.

The table defines a configuration block for **“bedding distribution in the plan view”** and related parameters that control how a halfspace (and optional layered/interpolated variants) is represented in a global coordinate system. It is organized as rows with columns **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**, where each item is a keyword used in the input file.

### Bedding distribution parameters
- **TYPE** (unit: —, default: **CONS**): Selects the bedding distribution model in plan view.
  - **CONS**: constant profile everywhere; bedding thickness and parameters do not vary spatially.
  - **COOR**: bedding varies by interpolating bore coordinates, using a **weight factor EP** (see below). This supports variable profiles based on bore definitions (e.g., an interpolation file such as `hase5_profile_interpolation.dat` is referenced in the context).
  - **LAYR**: “layered halfspace.” Soil stiffness and resistance parameters are taken from **BLAY** and interpolated onto a discrete 3D layered geometry (a triangular prism mesh) automatically generated from bore profile definitions. The mesh geometry is stored in an auxiliary database whose name is controlled by **NAME**.
- **EP** (unit: —, default: **1.5**): Weight factor used **only for TYPE = COOR** to influence how bore data are blended during interpolation.
- **Z** (unit: **m**, default: **0**): Defines the **surface level of the halfspace** in the global coordinate system.
- **ZVAR** (unit: —, default: **AUTO**): Controls whether the surface level of the halfspace varies via “variable surface level” logic described in chapter 2.
  - **NO**: QUADs below **Z** are not considered (excluded from halfspace contact).
  - **AUTO**: horizontal QUADs below **Z** are assigned halfspace contact, enabling automatic contact activation.

### Directional stiffness factors (horizontal bedding)
These factors scale stiffness contributions by direction and are typically used to model **horizontal bedding** behavior:
- **FAKX** (unit: —, default: **0.4**): stiffness factor in **x** direction.
- **FAKY** (unit: —, default: **0.4**): stiffness factor in **y** direction.
- **FAKZ** (unit: —, default: **1**): stiffness factor in **z** direction.
The context notes that FAKX/FAKY correspond to “horizontal stiffness” (chapter 2), enabling simulation of bedding anisotropy.

### Auxiliary database naming
- **NAME** (unit: default “—” in table, no default shown): Controls the database name related to secondary QUAD system or the **newly generated LAYR database** when TYPE = **LAYR**.
  - If NAME is not provided, the auxiliary *CDB is saved as **`$(nme)_yr.cdb`**, where `$(nme)` is the current project name.
  - The context references example interpolation file naming (e.g., `hase4_layr_interpolation.dat`) and that the 3D mesh geometry is saved under the specified NAME.

Overall, this table is a parameter specification for creating a halfspace-based bedding/contact model in plan view, supporting three main modes (constant, bore-interpolated, and layered/meshed), with additional control over contact activation below a reference surface and anisotropic stiffness scaling through FAKX/FAKY/FAKZ.

### Table description (for RAG / vector store)

This input table defines a single record field used to control **which bore profiles are selected** when forming a computational definition related to the “halfspace” concept (as referenced in the surrounding context). The table is structured with four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**.

#### Columns
- **Item (NO)**: Identifies the field name/keyword as **NO**.
- **Description**: States that the value represents the **“Numbers of selected bore profiles.”**
- **Unit (–)**: No measurement unit applies; the field is purely a count/selector quantity.
- **Default (!) **: The default is indicated as **“!”**, implying the value is mandatory or conditionally required (i.e., no explicit numeric default is provided in the table).

#### Meaning of the field “NO”
The value of **NO** determines **how many bore profiles are selected/used** by the processing component (in context, by HASE) to define the halfspace. It is therefore not the bore profile IDs themselves, but the **number of bore profiles** that will be included according to the interpolation strategy and/or other controlling records (such as **BORE** mentioned in the additional context).

#### Relationship to interpolation types (context)
The accompanying text specifies rules for selecting bore profiles depending on the interpolation type:
- For **CONS**: typically **only one** bore profile is used; if BORE is not specified, the smallest profile number is chosen; if multiple are defined, still the smallest is used.
- For **QUAD**: **all** bore profiles defined in AQUA that are used for the secondary QUAD system contribute to the halfspace; **BORE record is not used**.
- For **COOR**: requires **at least two** bore profiles when BORE is specified; otherwise all profiles defined in AQUA are used.
- For **LAYR**: requires **at least three** bore profiles when BORE is specified; otherwise all profiles defined in AQUA are used.

While this table does not directly state these thresholds, it is consistent with them: the **NO** field captures the **count** of bore profiles that the system will take into account under the chosen method.

#### Practical interpretation
When configuring the halfspace definition, **NO** must be set to a value consistent with the interpolation method’s minimum number of bore profiles (e.g., at least 2 for COOR and at least 3 for LAYR when applicable). Because the default is marked with **“!”**, the field should be treated as **required/critical** for correct setup.

See also: HALF
 BORE
 The record BORE specifies which bore profiles defined in AQUA are to be used by HASE for the definition of the halfspace. Depending on the type of the interpolation, the following applies:
 1. CONS - For this type of interpolation only one bore profile will be used for the definition of the halfspace. If BORE record is not specified, then a bore profile with smallest bore profile number (as defined in AQUA) will be selected. Similarly if more than one bore profile is defined with BORE record, bore profile with smallest bore profile number will be used.
 2. QUAD - BORE record is not used for this interpolation type. All bore profiles which are defined with AQUA and used for the generation of the secondary QUAD system will also be used for the definition of the halfspace.
 3. COOR - Minimum two bore profiles must be specified with BORE record. If nothing is specified, all bore profiles defined within AQUA are used for the interpolation.
 4. LAYR - Minimum three bore profiles must be specified for this method to be applied. As before, if nothing is specified, all bore profiles defined within AQUA are used.

The table describes the parameters of the HASE record **PILE** (internal HASE-piles). This record models how pile loads are introduced into the soil “internally” through stiffness/stress coefficients at the halfspace surface—i.e., the piles are **not discretized as beam elements**. The load transfer is based on **skin friction** along the pile shaft and a **pile foot** component, with different handling for linear vs. nonlinear calculations. The record is available only in the **expanded HASE version (HASE-3D)**.

**Column structure:** Each row corresponds to one input parameter (“Item”), with a short explanation, an expected unit (“Unit”), and a stated default value (“Default”). The table uses coordinate-based inputs for pile geometry and load-transfer behavior, and includes optional material definition for pile stiffness.

Key parameters:

- **X (m, default !)**: Either the pile coordinates or a **node number**. It specifies the horizontal position of the pile (depending on whether coordinates or nodes are used).
- **Y (m, default !)**: Used analogously to X. If **X = NNO**, then **Y = node number** is used to identify the location.
- **D0 (m, default D)**: **Pile diameter**. This is used to compute pile-related concrete surface/area effects in settlement calculations.
- **D (m, default !/1.5D0)**: **Pile foot diameter**. The table notes that the “effective stress due to settlement is determined directly under the pile foot with this diameter.” Default is given as **1/1.5 · D0** (i.e., approximately D = D0/1.5).
- **Z (m, default !)**: **Pile foot coordinate**, defining the depth/vertical position of the pile base in the halfspace.
- **MANT (–, default 0.50)**: Fraction of the **total pile load** transferred to soil as **shaft skin friction**. The remaining fraction is transferred via the pile foot component in the internal-pile formulation.
- **ZMAN (m, default *)**: Depth coordinate where **skin friction becomes active**. The default describes a model where skin friction is **inactive near the surface**, assuming that **25% of the pile length** starting from the surface does not transfer skin friction.
- **PMAM (kN, default –)**: **Maximum load transferable by skin friction**. This acts as a cap for the shaft contribution.
- **PMAF (kN, default –)**: **Maximum load transferable through the pile foot**. Importantly, **PMAM/PMAF apply only to nonlinear calculations**, and the table points to record **PLAS** for nonlinear-specific notes.
- **MNO (–, default –)**: **Material number of piles**. If provided, the pile’s elastic modulus comes from that material (e.g., relevant for vibrated piles); if not provided, the method assumes a default concrete modulus (as noted in the surrounding context: **28000 MN/m² for C30/37**).

Overall behavior tied to these inputs: the pile load is partitioned into shaft and foot contributions (linear case assumed to transfer total load to soil via skin friction and foot component; nonlinear case uses capacity limits PMAM/PMAF). For settlement, the table’s referenced context indicates that pile precompression is included using **Äl = N·l/EA** and that settlement calculations use concrete elastic modulus (28000 MN/m² unless MNO overrides) and compute concrete contact area from the pile diameter. The internal pile formulation relies on a halfspace load decomposition (Midlin solution) into compressive and tensile components under the applied load.

### Table: Non-linear halfspace soil parameters (Record **PLAS**)

This table summarizes the input items used to control *non-linear halfspace calculations* in the ASE program, specifically for the record **PLAS**. These parameters govern how the maximum allowable soil pressures (compression) develop both at the halfspace boundary and—optionally—throughout the slab interior, and they also include a friction-related parameter relevant to horizontal load effects at the bottom slab.

#### **Columns**
- **Item**: Parameter name used in the input records.
- **Description**: What the parameter represents mechanically.
- **Unit**: Physical unit of the parameter (or dimensionless if “–”).
- **Default**: Default value if the user does not provide an override.

---

## Parameters

### 1) **PMAX**
- **Meaning**: *Maximum bedding stress at the boundary of the halfspace*.
- **Behavior**: Defines the starting value of the compressive stress level that is valid for the entire halfspace boundary condition (i.e., it represents a positive compressive stress magnitude used as the initial limit for non-linear behavior).
- **Unit**: **kN/m²**
- **Default**: **– (not given)**  
  → Indicates this is typically user-supplied because it drives the maximum soil pressure level.

---

### 2) **DPDS**
- **Meaning**: *Factor controlling how the maximum compressive stress (max-sigma) increases toward the interior of the slab*.
- **Behavior**: Used to shape the evolution of the maximum bedding stress from the boundary into the slab interior using an **e-function** (exponential growth form).  
  - At the boundary: `max-sigma = PMAX`
  - Inside the slab: `max-sigma` increases with depth/distance according to the e-function scaled by **DPDS**.
- **Unit**: **– (dimensionless)**  
- **Default**: **– (not given)**  
  → Typically only meaningful if non-linear distribution through the slab interior is desired (often used together with PMAX).

---

### 3) **MUE**
- **Meaning**: *Friction value in the bottom slab for horizontal effects*.
- **Role in mechanics**: Provides the friction coefficient used for horizontal interaction effects at the bottom slab; this parameter affects mobilized resistance under horizontal loading.
- **Unit**: **– (dimensionless)**
- **Default**: **0.5**  
  → If omitted, ASE uses **0.5**.

---

### Overall interpretation for RAG
This table defines the key scalar controls that shape ASE’s non-linear halfspace response in record **PLAS**: **PMAX** sets the maximum compressive bedding stress at the boundary, **DPDS** modulates how that limit increases exponentially into the slab interior, and **MUE** supplies the friction coefficient for horizontal loading effects at the bottom slab.

See also: CTRL, HALF, PILE
 PLAS
 Non-linear halfspace calculations:
 The program ASE can be used to analyse the lifting of the bottom plate in a non- linear calcu- lation, as well as plasticizing at the plate edge and at the pile nodes.
 The record PLAS can be used to input a maximum soil pressure PMAX in kN/m2 for the bottom plate (which is valid over the entire halfspace). The input value represents a positive compressive stress.
 The following parameters can be specified for nonlinear calculations in ASE:
 • at halfspace nodes:
 compression: on input of PLAS: max. bedding max-sigma = PMAX (record PLAS)
 compression: with input of PLAS+DPDS you can simulate a phi and C of a soil. The max. bedding max-sigma can then increase starting from the boundary. Directly at the boundary, max-sigma starts with PLAS, to the interior of the slab max-sigma then increases with an e-function.
 Example PLAS=40 DPDS=1.8
 At the boundary: max-sigma =PLAS =40 kN/m2
 0.25 m inside: max-sigma 40 kN/m2*e0.25∗1.8 = 63 kN/m2
 1.00 m inside: max-sigma 40 kN/m2*e1.00∗1.8 = 240 kN/m2
 This DPDS e-function also works inside a slab e.g. at an internal gap as shown in example hase1_bottomslab.dat in loadcase 21 (linear) and 22 (nonlinear).
 tension: no tensile forces between the halfspace and the slab
 • at pile nodes:
 compression: max. pile force = PMAM+PMAF (record PILE)

 If the maximum pile foot force PMAF or the maximum skin friction force PMAM is reached before the maximum total pile force is reached PMAX=PMAM+PMAF (if MANT is not input as relation PMAM/PMAX), a plasticising will occur in ASE beginning at this load condition. The table defines the parameter set for a **LOAD** record, which applies a load for a settlement calculation on a halfspace. The parameters control *where* the load is applied and *its magnitude* along the Z-axis.

---

### Fields

#### 1) **NO** (Unit: —, Default: **!**)
- **Meaning:** Node number from which the load performs.  
- **Role in the calculation:** This identifies the starting point (a specific node) that determines the location/geometry of how the load is interpreted and applied within the halfspace model.
- **Special test behavior:** A notable case is when **NO = 0**. In that case, the system applies a **constant load** at **all halfspace QUAD elements** (useful for testing). Example given:  
  - `LC 101 ; LOAD NO 0 PZ 1.0`  
  This would apply `PZ = 1.0 kN` uniformly in the relevant direction to every QUAD element in the halfspace.

- **Default:** The “!” indicates **no default value is provided**—the node number is required.

---

#### 2) **PZ** (Unit: **kN**, Default: **0**)
- **Meaning:** Load value in the **Z direction**.
- **Role in the calculation:** Specifies the magnitude of the load component acting vertically (or along the model’s Z-axis). The load is interpreted as **untensioned** (as stated in the surrounding context for LOAD), and it is used in a separate settlement analysis (record **LC**).
- **Default:** If not specified, the load magnitude is **0 kN**, meaning no effect from the Z-direction load.

---

### Integration with overall LOAD behavior (context)
When an input uses **LOAD** within a load case (**LC**), the program executes a **separate settlement calculation** (see **LC**). The loads are interpreted for the **halfspace** directly; **stiffnesses from an FE system are not considered**. Additionally, if a load case number already exists, the corresponding record may be **deleted and recalculated** based on the new LOAD definition.

This means the table’s fields (**NO**, **PZ**) directly control the halfspace forcing used during that settlement computation, with **NO=0** offering a uniform test load across all QUAD elements.

See also: HALF, LC
 LOAD
 For an input of loads with LOAD a separate settlement calculation is executed (see record LC). The loads are interpreted as untensioned loads on the halfspace. The stiffnesses from a FE system are not considered. If a load case with the same number already exists, it will be deleted.
 One separate settlement analysis that can be used for test purposes is specifying the node number 0, which causes a constant load to be applied [e.g.: LC 101 ; LOAD NO 0 PZ 1.0] at all halfspace QUAD elements.

**Table columns**

---

### Parameter: **NO**

The table defines the input parameters for the **SELP** feature related to **storing results at depth and optionally generating BRIC outputs** (a separate database containing stress/settlement results mapped to BRIC elements).

### Items and meanings

- **ZR** *(Depth to be stored)*  
  Specifies the depth level at which the computed halfspace stresses are to be captured. It must be **≥ 0.0** and is defined **relative to the halfspace surface**.  
  **Unit:** not given (table shows “—”), but conceptually it is a depth coordinate relative to the halfspace surface.  
  **Default:** none (shown as “-”), i.e., must be provided when SELP ZR is used.

- **LCST** *(Load case storage number)*  
  Indicates the **load case ID** under which the stored bedding stresses (or related results) will be saved.  
  When records provide one LCST number without an accompanying depth Z, the system **automatically increments** load case numbers to create multiple load cases in one run.  
  **Unit:** —  
  **Default:** “!” (meaning required/validated; not a free default).

- **BRIC** *(File name for newly generated database)*  
  Provides the **file name** for an additional output database that is generated during the calculation. This new database contains **BRIC elements with stresses at the nodes**.  
  The BRIC elements are formed by **extruding QUAD elements** at the soil-structure interface.  
  **Default:** `LIT32` (table shows default value).  
  **Default marker “*”** likely indicates a conditional default or that it can be omitted depending on other inputs.

- **DX** *(Grid offset in x direction)*  
  Defines an **offset** used when creating a BRIC GRID system that extends beyond the interface bounding box.  
  **Unit:** m  
  **Default:** “!” (typically required/only meaningful when BRIC GRID creation is requested).

- **DY** *(Grid offset in y direction)*  
  Similar to DX, but for the y direction. Together with DX/DY, it enlarges the bounding box of the soil-structure interface for the generated grid.  
  **Unit:** m  
  **Default:** “!”  

- **HMIN** *(Minimum grid size)*  
  Controls the **minimum mesh spacing** used when generating the surface grid mesh that later gets extruded into BRIC elements.  
  **Unit:** m  
  **Default:** “!”

### How these parameters interact (context from description)

- Example behavior: when using something like **SELP ZR 5.0 LCST 1001**, stresses are calculated in the halfspace at **depth 5.0 m** and stored as **bedding stresses of QUAD elements** in **load case 101** (illustrating mapping between input depth, storage, and produced LC numbers).
- If **BRIC** is specified, a new **.cdb** file is generated (in addition to the LCST results). It stores **node stresses** in the extruded BRIC elements.
- If **DX, DY, and HMIN** are also defined and are **greater than zero**, the program creates a **BRIC GRID** database:
  1) find and extend the bounding box of the interface elements by **DX/DY**,  
  2) generate a regular surface grid mesh using **HMIN**,  
  3) extrude it to generate BRIC elements with stresses and settlements at nodes.

**Description**: “A literal from the following list.”  
This field selects **the output category / record type**. The allowed keywords are:

- **PROF**: Soil profile value  
- **PILE**: Pile elements

The input table is a per–halfspace output summary produced for **each halfspace definition** in the model. It can be suppressed with the option **“ECHO HALF NO.”** The table compiles both **geometric/identification parameters** of the halfspace and **numerical/mesh-contact statistics** used to set up stiffness/contact behavior. All values are associated with a specific halfspace partition, identified by the program’s records and internal halfspace indexing.

## Halfspace definition metadata
- **PROF (soil profile number):** The soil profile identifier from the record **BLAY** (program AQUA).
- **HALF:** The halfspace number as defined by the input “HALF number of layers from BLAY.”
- **Number of layers:** How many layers belong to this halfspace grouping.
- **Top-halfspace [m]:** The global vertical coordinate (height/depth) that marks the top of the halfspace.
- **Global Z coordinate min-load-radius [m] (from LOAR):** Minimum load radius position/extent associated with load application.
- **Beam-load-radius [m] (from LOAR):** Radius used for beam-related load influence.
- **Influence-radius [m] (default for beam nodes):** Default influence radius for beam nodes; it **reduces bandwidth of the stiffness matrix**, improving computational efficiency.
- **Direction of bedding (Factor):** A distribution factor indicating what percentage of stiffness (or bedding contribution) is stored in the **X, Y, and/or Z** directions. The entries are **directional components (X, Y, Z)** and sum to represent the total bedding directionality.

## Contact and mesh statistics
The table then reports counts and area sums related to the contact surface discretization at the halfspace:
- **contact area [m²]:** Total contact area, computed as **sum of all node areas**.
- **total number of nodes:** Total nodes considered in the contact-related discretization.
- **contact nodes at the top of halfspace:** Number of nodes that lie on the interface/top surface of the halfspace.
- **active quad nodes:** Number of QUAD nodes detected at the halfspace surface; these are used for surface-based computations such as load-radius determination.
- **active quad elements:** Number of QUAD surface elements found at the halfspace surface; explicitly noted as used for determining the **load radius** (load radius determination).
- **active quad area [m²]:** Sum of areas of all active QUAD elements on the interface.
- **beam nodes:** Number of nodes that do **not** have QUAD element connectivity (i.e., beam-only nodes in the surface representation).

## Bedding stress parameter
- **Maximum bedding stress for non-linear analysis:** The maximum bedding stress value taken from the record **PLAS**, reported in **kN/m²**. This is the governing limit used when non-linear bedding behavior is activated.

Overall, the table provides a compact “setup audit” for each halfspace: it links halfspace geometry and bedding direction settings with the actual discretized surface entities (nodes/elements/areas) and the key non-linear bedding stress limit.

Given a building which is idealized as a framework. The bottom plate lies on the ground, which is characterized by two soil layers each having a constant stiffness module. The soil parameters are constant over the plan view. Example - hase2_3d.dat
 The framework is composed of beams elements, and the bottom plate is entered as QUAD elements. Separate foundations are given at the nodes 1402 and 1406. Floor slabs are defined using QUAD elements to complete the load description and to represent the upper floor levels. (In this way the hidden line algorithm supplies more plastic pictures.)
 No fixities are specified in the input. The bottom plate lies at the level z = +2.00m (global Z coordinate).
 The soil profile is defined with the records BORE and BLAY and assigned soil profile number 3 (program AQUA). In the first layer from z = 2.00m to 4.80m, the stiffness modulus is set to 90Mp, and in the second layer only 30Mp. Beneath the global Z coordinate of 9.80m, it is assumed the ground is perfectly rigid. This ends the description of the soil profile.
 +PROG AQUA
 HEAD !... BORE 3 BLAY 2.00 ES 90000 BLAY 4.80 ES 30000 BLAY 9.80 ES 30000 !... END
 BORE 3
 The half space is now described in HASE:
 +PROG HASE
 HEAD FORMATION OF THE HALFSPACE STIFFNESS MATRIX HALF TYPE CONS PROF 3 Z 2.00 FAKX 1 FAKY 1 FAKZ 1 LOAR BEAM 0.70
 END
 The stiffness is stored in all three directions with FAKX 1 1 1. This precludes the necessity to later specify horizontal fixings. The horizontal loads are distributed over the bottom plate and thereby transferred to the building ground.
